parts.article:
Learning to Walk
 
A These days the feet of a typical city dweller rarely encounter terrain any more uneven than a crack in the pavement. While that may not seem like a problem, it turns out that by flattening our urban environment we have put ourselves at risk of a surprising number of chronic illnesses and disabilities. Fortunately, the commercial market has come to the rescue with a choice of products. Research into the idea that flat floors could be detrimental to our health was pioneered back in the late 1960s in Long Beach, California. Podiatrist Charles Brantingham and physiologist Bruce Beekman were concerned with the growing epidemic of high blood pressure, varicose veins and deep-vein thromboses and reckoned they might be linked to the uniformity of the surfaces that we tend to stand and walk on.
 
B The trouble, they believed, was that walking continuously on flat floors, sidewalks and streets concentrates forces on just a few areas of the foot. As a result, these surfaces are likely to be far more conducive to chronic stress syndromes than natural surfaces, where the foot meets the ground in a wide variety of orientations. They understood that the anatomy of the foot parallels that of the human hand - each having 26 bones, 33 joints and more than 100 muscles, tendons and ligaments - and that modern lifestyles waste all this potential flexibility.
 
C Brantingham and Beekman became convinced that the damage could be rectified by making people wobble. To test their ideas, they got 65 factory workers to try standing on a variable terrain floor - spongy mats with varying degrees of resistance across the surface. This modest irregularity allowed the soles of the volunteers’ feet to deviate slightly from the horizontal each time they shifted position. As the researchers hoped, this simple intervention made a huge difference, within a few weeks. Even if people were wobbling slightly, it activated a host of muscles in their legs, which in turn helped pump blood back to their hearts. The muscle action prevented the pooling of blood in their feet and legs, reducing the stress on the heart and circulation. Yet decades later, the flooring of the world's largest workplaces remains relentlessly smooth. Earlier this year, however, the idea was revived when other researchers in the US announced findings from a similar experiment with people over 60. John Fisher and colleagues at the Oregon Research Institute in Eugene designed a mat intended to replicate the effect of walking on cobblestones*.
 
D In tests funded by the National Institute of Aging, they got some 50 adults to walk on the mats in their bare feet for less than an hour, three times a week. After 16 weeks, these people showed marked improvements in mobility, and even a significant reduction in blood pressure. People in a control group who walked on ordinary floors also improved but not as dramatically. The mats are now available for purchase and production is being scaled up. Even so, demand could exceed supply if this foot-stimulating activity really is a ‘useful nonpharmacological approach for preventing or controlling hypertension of older adults, as the researchers believe. They are not alone in recognising the benefits of cobblestones. Reflexologists have long advocated walking on textured surfaces to stimulate so-called ‘acupoints’ on the soles of the feet. They believe that pressure applied to particular spots on the foot connects directly to particular organs of the body and somehow enhances their function. In China, spas, apartment blocks and even factories promote their cobblestone paths as healthful amenities. Fisher admits he got the concept from regular visits to the country. Here, city dwellers take daily walks along cobbled paths for five or ten minutes, perhaps several times a day, to improve their health. The idea is now taking off in Europe too.
 
E People in Germany, Austria and Switzerland can now visit ‘barefoot parks’ and walk along ‘paths of the senses - with mud, logs, stone and moss underfoot. And it is not difficult to construct your own path with simple everyday objects such as stones or bamboo poles. But if none of these solutions appeal, there is another option. A new shoe on the market claims to transform flat, hard, artificial surfaces into something like uneven ground. ‘These shoes have an unbelievable effect,’ says Benno Nigg, an exercise scientist at Calgary University in Canada.
 
F Known as the Masai Barefoot Technology, the shoes have rounded soles that cause you to rock slightly when you stand still, exercising the small muscles around the ankle that are responsible for stability. Forces in the joint are reduced, putting less strain on the system, Nigg claims.
 
G Some of these options may not appeal to all consumers and there is a far simpler alternative. If the urban environment is detrimental to our health, then it is obvious where we should turn. A weekend or even a few hours spent in the countryside could help alleviate a sufferer’s aches and pains, and would require only the spending of time. However, for many modern citizens, the countryside is not as accessible as it once was and is in fact a dwindling resource. Our concrete cities are growing at a terrifying rate - perhaps at the same rate as our health problems.
parts.questions:
Questions 27-31
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage?
In boxes 27-31 on your answer sheet, write:

Q27 Brantingham and Beekman were the first researchers to investigate the relationship between health problems and flat floors.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q28 The subjects in Fisher's control group experienced a decline in their physical condition.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q29 The manufacturers are increasing the number of cobblestone mats they are making.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q30 Fisher based his ideas on what he saw during an overseas trip.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q31 The Masai Barefoot Technology shoes are made to fit people of all ages.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
Write the correct letter in boxes 32-34 on your answer sheet.

Q32 The writer suggests that Brantingham and Beekman's findings were

  • A ignored by big companies.
  • B doubted by other researchers.
  • C applicable to a narrow range of people.
  • D surprising to them.

Q33 What claim is made by the designers of the cobblestone mats"?

  • A They need to be used continuously in order to have a lasting effect.
  • B They would be as beneficial to younger people as to older people.
  • C They could be an effective alternative to medical intervention.
  • D Their effects may vary depending on individual users.

Q34 Which of the following points does the writer make in the final paragraph?

  • A People should question new theories that scientists put forward.
  • B High prices do not necessarily equate to a quality product.
  • C People are setting up home in the country for health reasons.
  • D The natural environment is fast disappearing.
Questions 35-40
Complete the summary below.
Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.
In their research, Brantingham and Beekman looked at the complex physical of the foot and noted that the surfaces of modern environments restrict its movement. They invented a mat which they tried out on factory workers. Whenever the workers walked on it, the different levels of in the mat would encourage greater muscle action. In turn, this lessened the effect of on the cardiovascular system.
Similar research was undertaken by John Fisher and colleagues in Oregon. As a result of their findings, they decided to market cobblestone mats to the elderly as a means of dealing with . Reflexologists claim that by manipulating specific parts of the feet, the performance of certain will also improve. Finally, Benno Nigg at Calgary University believes that specially shaped on shoes should give health benefits.

reference:
Q27

干扰 你可能觉得“pioneered”不代表就是全球第一人，但在雅思阅读中，这个词就是对应题目中“the first”的核心考点。

句子 (A段) Research into the idea that flat floors could be detrimental to our health was pioneered back in the late 1960s in Long Beach, California. Podiatrist Charles Brantingham and physiologist Bruce Beekman were concerned with the growing epidemic of high blood pressure, varicose veins and deep-vein thromboses and reckoned they might be linked to the uniformity of the surfaces that we tend to stand and walk on.

解析 原文明确提到这两位研究者在20世纪60年代末“率先（pioneered）”研究了平坦地面可能对健康有害的观点。

Q28

解析 原文说控制组的人身体状况也“有所改善（improved）”，而不是题目说的“下降（decline）”。

干扰 你可能看到“not as dramatically”就以为他们变差了，其实他们只是进步得慢一点，方向依然是变好。

句子 (D段) After 16 weeks, these people showed marked improvements in mobility, and even a significant reduction in blood pressure. People in a control group who walked on ordinary floors also improved but not as dramatically.

Q29

解析 原文提到这种垫子现在可以购买，并且“生产规模正在扩大（production is being scaled up）”。

干扰 只要看到“scaled up”，就直接对应题目里的“increasing the number”，不要纠结具体的增长数量。

句子 (D段) The mats are now available for purchase and production is being scaled up. Even so, demand could exceed supply if this foot-stimulating activity really is a ‘useful nonpharmacological approach for preventing or controlling hypertension of older adults, as the researchers believe.

Q30

句子 (D段) In China, spas, apartment blocks and even factories promote their cobblestone paths as healthful amenities. Fisher admits he got the concept from regular visits to the country.

解析 Fisher承认他的灵感来自于“经常访问那个国家（regular visits to the country）”，即前文提到的中国（China）。

干扰 你要能把文中的“China”和题目中的“overseas trip”联系起来，去国外旅游/访问就属于海外行程。

Q31

解析 文章提到了这种鞋的效果和原理，但完全没有提到它是否适合“所有年龄段”的人。

干扰 你可能会因为看到它能锻炼脚踝肌肉就默认老少皆宜，但文章没写的事情绝对不能自己脑补。

句子 (F段) Known as the Masai Barefoot Technology, the shoes have rounded soles that cause you to rock slightly when you stand still, exercising the small muscles around the ankle that are responsible for stability. Forces in the joint are reduced, putting less strain on the system, Nigg claims.

Q32

解析 作者感叹几十年后世界上最大型工作场所的地面依然是“无情的平滑（relentlessly smooth）”，暗示这些发现被大公司无视了。

干扰 你可能想选B，但文中只说研究在几十年后才被“重新提起（revived）”，并没说其他研究者怀疑它。

句子 (C段) The muscle action prevented the pooling of blood in their feet and legs, reducing the stress on the heart and circulation. Yet decades later, the flooring of the world's largest workplaces remains relentlessly smooth.

Q33

解析 研究人员认为这是一种预防或控制高血压的“非药物方法（nonpharmacological approach）”，即医疗手段之外的有效替代方案。

干扰 你要识别出“nonpharmacological（非药理/非药物）”对应选项中的“alternative to medical intervention”。

句子 (D段) Even so, demand could exceed supply if this foot-stimulating activity really is a ‘useful nonpharmacological approach for preventing or controlling hypertension of older adults, as the researchers believe.

Q34

干扰 虽然文中提到了城市在扩张，但作者的核心落脚点在于自然环境正在快速消失。

句子 (G段) However, for many modern citizens, the countryside is not as accessible as it once was and is in fact a dwindling resource. Our concrete cities are growing at a terrifying rate - perhaps at the same rate as our health problems.

解析 最后一段明确提到农村/大自然不再像以前那样容易到达，且是一种“正在萎缩的资源（dwindling resource）”。

Q35

解析 原文提到他们理解脚部的“解剖结构（anatomy）”与人手相似，都有很多骨头和肌肉。

干扰 这个词出现在B段，用来描述脚部复杂的物理构造。

句子 (B段) They understood that the anatomy of the foot parallels that of the human hand - each having 26 bones, 33 joints and more than 100 muscles, tendons and ligaments - and that modern lifestyles waste all this potential flexibility.

Q36

解析 工人们站在海绵垫上，这些垫子表面具有“不同程度的阻力（varying degrees of resistance）”。

干扰 题目里的“different levels of”对应原文的“varying degrees of”。

句子 (C段) To test their ideas, they got 65 factory workers to try standing on a variable terrain floor - spongy mats with varying degrees of resistance across the surface.

Q37

句子 (C段) The muscle action prevented the pooling of blood in their feet and legs, reducing the stress on the heart and circulation.

解析 通过肌肉运动促进血液回流，从而“减轻了对心脏和循环系统的压力（reducing the stress）”。

干扰 注意题目中是“cardiovascular system（心血管系统）”，对应文中的“heart and circulation”。

Q38

解析 研究人员向老年人推广这种垫子，作为控制“高血压（hypertension）”的方法。

干扰 高血压在文中出现了两次，一次是“high blood pressure”，一次是专业词汇“hypertension”，填空要找对应位置的单词。

句子 (D段) Even so, demand could exceed supply if this foot-stimulating activity really is a ‘useful nonpharmacological approach for preventing or controlling hypertension of older adults, as the researchers believe.

Q39

解析 足疗师认为按压脚部特定点可以增强身体特定“器官（organs）”的功能。

干扰 原文中“connects directly to particular organs”直接对应了题目。

句子 (D段) They believe that pressure applied to particular spots on the foot connects directly to particular organs of the body and somehow enhances their function.

Q40

解析 Benno Nigg提到的这种鞋拥有“圆形的鞋底（rounded soles）”，能产生健康益处。

干扰 题目问的是鞋上的什么东西被特殊塑形了，原文明确指出的部位是“soles”。

句子 (F段) Known as the Masai Barefoot Technology, the shoes have rounded soles that cause you to rock slightly when you stand still, exercising the small muscles around the ankle that are responsible for stability.
